articles.title: Anthropology and Politics
articles.description: The Joint Honours Programme in Anthropology and Politics provides students with an in-depth, interdisciplinary understanding of contemporary cultures and politics, international affairs, societies, and institutions in their political, historical, social, cultural, economic and legal dimensions. Anthropology is the study of human diversity around the world. In studying anthropology, you will learn how different societies live together and think about such topics as family, religion, art, politics and economics and gain skills increasingly in demand in a globalized and automated world. Studying anthropology at Queen’s will allow you to examine through working closely with people on the ground some of the deepest and most pressing questions about human beings. Issues addressed in our modules include: Does globalisation mean the end of cultural difference? Can a post-conflict society heal? How do ritual traditions, musical performances, and art shape cultural identities? How do some people become willing to die for a group? Through classroom modules, optional placements, and your own anthropological fieldwork, you will also gain valuable skills in critical thinking, cross-cultural understanding, researching, interviewing, writing, and presenting. The academic study of politics is concerned with the sources of conflict, co-operation, power and decision-making within and between societies, how differences are expressed through ideology and organisation, and how, if at all, disagreements and problems are resolved. We look at conflict, co-operation and its origins, dynamics and trajectories, at theories of society, at the value and ethical basis of political ideas and action, and at politics in different national and historical contexts.

articles.title: Britain's swimming pool crisis unmasked with one facility closing each fortnight: 'Hugely damaging!'
articles.description: Britain is in the middle of a swimming pool crisis, with one facility closing every fortnight and hundreds at risk of shutting up shop for good. More than 500 pools were lost between 2010 and 2025 amid squeezed council budgets, according to the GMB union — and more than 1,200 are past their expected lifespans, leaving dozens of communities with hardly any places to swim. Philip Browning, Head of Public Affairs at Swim England, the sport's national governing body, said the long-term effects could be "hugely damaging" for the nation's health. He told GB News: "Already a quarter of all local authorities in England are short of the pool space they need by at least one swimming pool. Swimming is one of the few activities that can be done by people of all ages, from zero to 100, and remains one of the most popular activities in England, with over 12 million adults swimming each year." Swimming particularly supports older adults due to it being a non-weight-bearing, low-impact exercise, helping those with joint conditions, long-term injuries, or chronic pain. Some two million over-65s swim each year. Around 20 per cent of adults with a disability or long-term health condition also participate in the sport annually. James and Alice Gilbert, who recently took up swimming at the age of 65, told the People's Channel: "We have noticed some weight loss, which has been great. Over time, there's definitely been an increase in stamina and fewer aches and pains everywhere. It has improved our quality of life significantly. We've also found it clears our mind and gives us time to unwind – it makes us feel more invigorated." Swimming is also a life-saving skill, particularly for youngsters learning to dive into the water for the first time. At least 196 children died by drowning between 2019 and 2025, figures from the National Child Mortality Database show. LATEST SPORTS NEWS Michael Carrick sacked as Manchester United manager following torrid start to season Prince William asks Unai Emery about Villa 'every day' as Spaniard opens up on pair's relationship Liverpool star labels Harry Kane as an 'inspiration' following Ballon d'Or win Baroness Sharron Davies, the former Team GB athlete who learnt to swim at a public lido in Plymouth before earning silver at the 1980 Olympics in Moscow, told Britain's News Channel more attention must be given to young people, saying: "We've left primary schools; we're not even getting half of our kids swimming and that's utterly disgraceful. "We don't think outside the box; things have changed – it was easier to get to local pools. A lot of little primary schools had swimming pools, or the comprehensive associated with them had pools. They didn't spend all day putting kids on a bus, driving them down the road, and undressing and dressing them again in the pool. "Most of those sessions are an absolute waste of time. You've got 30 kids and eventually they get 10 minutes before they're all hurried back out again and back on a bus again. "We've got to think outside the box about how we get kids swimming in schools. One of my big projects is to try and get PE teachers back into primary schools, so that we can get kids more physically active in the early learning years when they put down all their habits. We have destroyed school sport." In 2024, Sport England found a third of pupils cannot swim 25 metres unaided when they leave primary school — a seven per cent increase on 2017 — due to prolonged pool closures caused by the coronavirus pandemic and high swimming lesson fees. To make matters worse, the UK had 12,000 vacant positions for swimming teachers in 2023, with roughly 600,000 children missing out on lessons. Baroness Davies "worries terribly" the mass exodus of pools "will only cause more harm". She added: "We're an island, surrounded by water and rivers and canals and quarries and God knows what. So, there are all sorts of reasons why it's imperative that we have swimming pools. I worry terribly about the fitness of our young people and their sort of resilience, which can come from sport; it's one of those wonderful things that teaches you great resilience." These knock-on effects could lead to a decline in elite sports stars, leaving emerging talent with fewer places to train. British swimmers have won 84 Olympic medals in the pool, with Adam Ramsay-Peaty, 31, contributing to three golds. Queen's Leisure Centre in Derby, where Ramsay-Peaty trained, was forced to close after operating for 90 years. It closed down in 2022 and has been at risk of demolition ever since. Repair costs at the venue were estimated to be around £10million, with Derby City Council exploring options to develop housing on the site. Swimming in the long term helps the National Health Service and Government, according to Mr Browning. He revealed: "Every £1 invested in the sport and exercise sector, £4.38 is generated via savings to the NHS, chronic illness prevention, improved workforce productivity and enhanced health and happiness. In addition, £14billion in tax revenue is generated by grassroots sport and exercise every year, a return of approximately six to seven times the public investment in sport and exercise." The problems these pools face are complex, resulting in exorbitant fees. The average cost to keep a pool going ranges from £500,000 to £1.5million per annum and the figure is only increasing. Hundreds of pools are past their expected lifespan and keeping them running is becoming a recurring issue for owners. Local authorities across the UK in the 1970s and 80s invested heavily in indoor public swimming pools, yet most of that infrastructure has not been replaced or modernised. Director of Research, Policy and Communications at UKActive, Clemency Lion, stated: "It's about 60 per cent of swimming pools are past their healthy lifespan in terms of the facilities that they're in. "Public leisure has got a really big problem with ageing infrastructure and there's a huge amount of investment that's needed to put into those ageing facilities to basically refresh them – make them where they need to be again. "So that's the kind of underlying issue. And then where you've got this ageing infrastructure, the costs of running those facilities also then go up because it's not so easy to put in place those more sustainable, environmentally friendly but also more cost-effective measures in place around an older pool." Several hot summers have also had an impact on pools, with millions of Britons being placed under severe drought conditions. In August, Southern Water applied to the Government for permission to issue a "non-essential use ban" in Hampshire and the Isle of Wight. The ban would have prevented private pools from being filled, not just public spaces. The global energy shock sparked by conflict in Eastern Europe and the Middle East has inflated these running costs, with many pools receiving little to no support. Ms Lion, a former special adviser at the Department for Environment Food and Rural Affairs, explained Sport England and the Government offered some respite during this period, but she felt it was only a "short-term" fix. She went on to say: "We're obviously in another period of energy prices going up. There's a level of protection those pools have built around themselves, but the longer this goes on, the more susceptible they'll be. They're going to come out of the contracts that they're in and then need to go into another one, which is going to be a much higher contract cost. "So, energy prices are definitely one that has impacted previously, and if things continue the way that they are, they are going to have a big impact again in the not-so-distant future." Despite these costs, swimming pools are not listed by the state as an "energy-intensive industry (EII)", which saw them miss out on benefits from John Healey's inaugural Autumn Budget. These include focused electricity price relief and a policy cost freeze, as the Chancellor laid out policies to address the energy crisis. Ms Lion stated if pools had been classified as an EII, it "would have relieved cost pressures". She commented: "That classification would go some way to supporting them to continue to run and stay open. I think it's something to look at. I would call on the Energy Secretary to review the categorisation of swimming pools and see whether there is a longer-term solution to the impact that energy-price fluctuations are having on swimming pools." Mr Browning echoed Ms Lion's points, outlining the social and economic benefits people will have in having more pools, stating: "The Government needs to invest in the pools we need for the future, both to help refurbish existing pools where appropriate, but to build the next generation of pools. "It previously announced £400million for grassroots sport, but so far none of that has gone on supporting swimming pools. Beyond that funding, we need to see a national facilities strategy, backed by funding, to deliver the network of pools we need for the future. "Doing so will not only help people live happier and healthier lives and reduce tragic drowning instances, it will pay itself back many times over and help the economy. "Inactivity currently costs the UK economy £20billion a year. By investing in the leisure centres and swimming pools that people want to use to be active, we can play a central role in tackling that." During her time at No10, Rachel Reeves announced 350 communities would benefit from additional support for pools, listing Blackpool South, Stockport, Stoke Central, Swindon North, Newcastle Upon Tyne East and Wallsend when delivering the news. All these areas have Labour MPs, with Conservative and Liberal Democrat politicians repeatedly criticising the Government for letting the £80million Swimming Pool Support Fund expire without a replacement. Responding to the criticism yesterday, Lisa Nandy, the Digital, Culture, Media and Sport Secretary, told the Commons ministers will create a new system to support "public leisure facilities". Speaking in the chamber, she told MPs: "I can tell the House that we are creating a public leisure facilities programme that will provide support for lidos and other swimming facilities, and that, thanks to the work that he and others have done to campaign for this, the programme will include the first dedicated fund for lidos that this country has produced."
